en: At his menace, men died of fright,
His visage blazed with wrath,
No man could endure approaching him,
A man spoken of like a wild beast,
Such a man stood there.
His executioners numbered seven hundred,
He had four thousand nobles,
His guards had their appointed fortune,
They stood with swords drawn.
Guards for the treasury,
Finishing their words, they fell silent,
The short of the angry words was this,
The chiefs who would not disperse,
When the decree remained, he cried out,
He had risen since the dawn,
They would not tell him to turn back to his horse,
They would not go and cause distress,
Now among the Chinese of forty kinds,
His disordered muttering,
They would not remain to turn back with a shout.
Ever a khan to the enemy people,
Murmuring in submission,
Pouring out and raking over your airs,
Cast down beneath,
His splendor looked like a mountain,
With arms as massive as a cart,
His excellence was his courage,
He appeared as one son of humankind.
Here too were two khans,
Now the chosen ones of the forty clans,
The son of the forty maidens,
The gathered Chinese stood watching,
We were the ones who stood out,
Here stood Ysyk-Tekur,
Was he the blue-maned gray,
One grave word from Koloy,
As though endowed with great courage,
Did the great one go striking with his sword,
As though he went with the valiant one.
When the third stood here,
To continue the tale briefly,
Of the Chinese, of distant Kakan,
He gathered its teeming people,
When Suurman stood there,
There was no one to turn them back,
His treasury remained unbroken,
When he took the reckoning,
There was no city besides Kakan,
When the teeming Chinese remained,
Third, to Dyisha,
His son, the city’s herald,
The khan’s night had fallen,
There was no one at all to guard the frontier,
Look closely: this people is Beijing,
Koloy’s grim, dark might,
This black host belongs to Dyisha,
He has a people swarming like black worms,
All the people of forty tribes are there,
The elder of all the people,
The ablest of the spearmen,
The finest of those who mount the troop,
This is the pasha of Beijing,
The tent of the watchman,
The hero of the people of Kakan,
Together with Suurulma and Chyng Tengir,
There are two heroes who win the horses,
Their names resound among the people,
They are a blessing to us,
There is a pair of heroes,
While the two of us stand here,
Would some grim mighty foe confront us?
Would one who has gone as an equal strike us?
Could an enemy break the heroes?
Would a man turn back without dying?
The people called him their enemy,
No living soul had defeated his might,
The lineage of two daughters,
A descendant of brave Kökchö,
His thought of the enemy was keen,
Of these scattered Burut people,
Look at the descendant who remained,
They say they set out upon that journey,
This fleeting world of seven days,
They say its course is sorrow,
The person who goes does not return,
He has entered the dark grave,
Word passes down from sage to sage,
The finest of them, a young champion,
From the great branch that would remain with Kerimche,
I heard that no offspring remained,
Among peoples of many different ranks,
One named Kenen was born,
I heard that a descendant remained.
Making Ala-Too his homeland,
I heard that Kongur remained,
When he went to Karakuman,
When Kaltai attacked from his side,
Fleeing, he saved the khan alive,
Laying a claim against Kaltai,
I heard that he took his blood in vengeance.
Advancing three times from the right flank,
They say he waged a boundless battle,
Firing the great jazayil and the bow,
They say the wretched Kyrgyz attacked.
The Örötkül came and moved around them,
The Chinese who went unpunished,
Ambushing them in a hidden place and striking them down,
Scattering all their possessions,
The Örötkül then turned back.
Turning back the edge of that host,
Their hero was Badykan,
That glaring Chinese warrior,
With no soul left to answer back,
That ill-fated eagle,
Casting them down as though slaughtered,
Without looking any man in the face,
Black-headed and fork-footed,
Unable to reckon a man worth even coarse cloth,
Having every passerby bound,
Bringing down the leopard-like khan.
From the man who went to meet them,
He has wrung the news from him.
His heroism and princely bearing,
He is a warrior better than them all,
A man who traveled there has seen him,
To every eye that beholds him, he is wondrous,
He roamed among peoples and reconnoitered lands,
The riders who went to gather news
Lost their wits,
Saddling their horses and making ready,
The hero, a moon-bright eagle,
Set out at that very time.
Making camp at a lodging place,
Taking the spoils that lay spread out,
Yielding no ground when surrounded,
Submitting to no man of courage,
They settled in Talas as their land.
If we make a nest for the shamed,
If we ask among the hills,
He had drawn close to the Chinese,
Red gold and white silver coins,
Saying he would seize it from the land,
Flaming up like a white gale,
Grieving, he would close his eyes,
Those who pursued him pressed onward,
Softening that people,
They say he found it as he had hoped,
Coming thoughtfully to the barren shore,
They say he found what lay at the root of his thought.
Like Manas, over Afghanistan,
He crushed its turmoil,
He scattered its four kinds of livestock,
Binding its claim through hunger,
Entering from Karak toward its mountain,
Tethering his mares on its pasture,
He bore down upon them from above,
He crushed their nobles,
Taking the booty and that people he found,
He subdued the four who had found shelter,
He scattered their four kinds of livestock,
The Afghan domain he had set his mind upon,
Without turning the reins toward the seat of honor,
There, standing exposed, their spirit broke,
He turned back the Afghan herds.
At that time, that people,
Saying the gray wolf had moved them away,
Turned every one of their necks.
A small number of Muslims,
Saying, “I shall make it a shrine,”
Having once been born into the world,
Saying he had come upon the face of the earth,
Making his court in Kokand,
Making that one into a shrine,
He set it close to paradise,
Losing sight of the white yurts,
Taking Afghanistan and Konguz,
Making that one a saint,
He laid out his paradise wide.
Gathering around a corrupt man,
Whatever ears had heard and eyes had seen,
Of distant Khodynch,
The finest of the Khakanians was its khan,
Among the Chinese people of forty khans,
There were a thousand watchful eyes,
There was a gray-maned hero to rule the people,
To all of Khodynch,
Sending word by a written notice,
The nobles Ebei and Shygai,
He set the Kazakhs marching against the Khakan,
Every living soul gathered,
The Chinese who had drawn their swords,
The Chinese people of forty khans,
Gathered in Beijing,
In this Beijing upon which radiance poured,
In this inexhaustible land,
There then stood the Old Khan,
Before the eyes of the Old Khan,
The one who became khan over ten khans,
When two thousand years had been fulfilled,
The Old Khan lived long,
When he was among the people,
Born in Altai and grown mighty,
His people gazed their fill at him, moonlike,
They saw no defect in his stature,
He became a match for foreign peoples,
His spoken word brought contentment,
The forty tribes of China, to the Khakan,
Paid neither tribute nor tax,
And did not heed the word he spoke.
Without treading the road that was laid out,
He would leave them a land of pursuit,
Without looking to the one who drove them,
He would set the people fighting behind him,
He set fighter against fighter in combat,
The age was thrown into disorder and strife,
To the Khakan with a horse-length host,
Keep laying siege, he said,
I shall encircle them all, one by one,
A soul lamenting over what had happened,
Wherever authority had arisen,
A mottled khan arose from the people,
He showed the enemy in the distance,
A man came forth bearing news.
Manas, lion of the people, had arisen,
Do you call only that one Manas?
A hero called Semetey arose,
Azhybai and Seytek arose as his equals,
However many fenced clans split apart,
All of them struck out straight from China,
We issued the command: go there,
What hero Seytek had seen,
Khan Zholtoi had gone at their head,
The great son-in-law of rich Kongur,
A fortunate son-in-law in all he did,
What a mighty son-in-law he was,
From the tidings of the dark warrior,
A wakeful soul was here,
The hero recognized the burning words,
This was Beijing’s backbone,
This lion was its own true son,
This was his surpassing place and station,
No word could touch him even for a month,
Black Zholtoi was undone,
This was the one who had seen so many wonders.
Looking at him, he closed his eyes,
Indeed, this is the enemy himself,
On earth he encountered a spirit,
To the Burut whom the black earth swallowed,
I have gone—yet the soul endures,
To this accursed people,
Having asked, it became a robe for him,
He did not cease from asking,
When he took the lance, it became an arrow,
If he drove them in the darkness,
There was an enemy like one who had fallen upon them,
Yours became eighty-four,
